passage: Behind the counter of his family's small shop in the kasba, Uday had learned to watch smiles. The wholesaler, Harsha, came in each Tuesday and greeted him with a quick, tight smile that stopped at the mouth. The old woman who bought tea leaves gave a slow one that crinkled her eyes and stayed for a while. Uday used to think the first meant "I dislike you." Today he wasn't sure. Harsha looked tired, then dropped an extra packet of biscuits on the counter and said, "For the kids you tutor." That smile came late and quiet. Uday noted it: the face was only a clue. He still asked, "Long journey today?" "Very," Harsha said.

qa.q: When does Harsha come into the shop?
qa.a: Harsha comes in each Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Uday thinking about Harsha's tight smile?
qa.a: He used to read it as dislike, but now he sees it might just be tiredness, since Harsha then did something kind.

qa.q: Why did Uday ask 'Long journey today?'
qa.a: A smile alone is only a rough clue, so a friendly question helps him check what is actually going on.

qa.q: How might Harsha see that tight smile?
qa.a: Harsha may simply be tired after travelling and not realise the smile looks polite and distant.

grounding: A young adult tells a polite mouth-only smile from a warm smile that involves the eyes, but treats it only as a rough clue.

passage: Bilal worked evenings at a small cafe in Warsaw, and he'd started noticing smiles the way some people notice weather. The manager's smile when she praised him was wide and instant, but it left her eyes untouched, and he wondered if it was only routine. A regular, Marek, gave a small smile, hardly more than a twitch, but it lasted and his eyes creased as he took his coffee. Bilal couldn't say which of the two was sincere. The manager's had felt fake, but she had actually given him a raise. Marek's quiet one had seemed genuine, and he had brought Bilal a jar of plum jam. He decided a smile was only a hint, and kept watching what people did.

qa.q: Where did Bilal work in the evenings?
qa.a: He worked evenings at a small cafe in Warsaw.

qa.q: What does Bilal suspect about the manager's smile, and why is he unsure?
qa.a: He wondered if her wide, instant smile was only routine, since her eyes were untouched, but he couldn't be sure because she had given him a raise.

qa.q: What did Bilal decide to do about reading smiles?
qa.a: He decided a smile is only a hint and kept watching what people actually did over time.

qa.q: How might Marek see his own small smile?
qa.a: He probably meant it warmly, though it was quiet, which shows that many genuine smiles are subtle.

grounding: A young adult compares a polite mouth-only smile with a warm eye-crinkling one, treating the difference as a rough clue only.

passage:
In her first week as a trainee at the bank branch in Indore, Madhuri tried to read her manager, Saurabh, all the time.
When she brought him the first report, he smiled quickly, mouth only, and said, "Thanks, put it there." Her heart dropped. Was it bad?
On Wednesday, when she solved a customer's problem at the counter, he watched and smiled differently: slower, his eyes crinkling at the corners. "Nicely handled."
She started keeping a mental list: quick smile equals polite, slow eye smile equals real.
But on Friday, when he gave her the busiest counter, he didn't smile at all. Just nodded. She panicked. Then a colleague told her, "That's his biggest compliment. He only gives that counter to people he trusts."
Madhuri stopped trusting her list. She asked him for feedback instead. He said, "You're doing well. I'm just not a big smiler."

qa.q: Where was Madhuri a trainee?
qa.a: At the bank branch in Indore.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when Saurabh gave only a quick smile?
qa.a: Madhuri felt anxious and worried, reading the mouth-only smile as a sign the report was bad.

qa.q: What did Madhuri learn about reading smiles?
qa.a: That the difference between polite and warm smiles is only a rough clue, so asking for feedback is more reliable.

qa.q: How did the colleague see Saurabh's nod on Friday?
qa.a: The colleague saw it as his biggest compliment, a sign of trust, even without a smile.

grounding: The scene shows a young adult reading polite and genuine smiles as clues, then learning that a quiet expression can still be warm.

passage:
Subject: Dinner with Riya's parents - help me read this

Tushar,
You're the only one I can ask. Last night I finally met Riya's parents. Her mother smiled at me the whole evening. Big smile, but, I swear, only her mouth moved. Her eyes stayed kind of still. Her father barely smiled at all, but when I talked about my grandfather's farm, his eyes lit up and he laughed properly.
So now I'm confused. Does her mother secretly not like me? Does her father actually like me?
I read somewhere that real smiles use the eyes. But Riya says her mother is just shy with new people and smiles like that at everyone, even her own sister.
I know it's a rough clue, not proof. I'm trying not to overthink. But I'm overthinking.
Should I just ask Riya what they said after I left? Or is that weird?
Harish

qa.q: When did Harish talk about his grandfather's farm?
qa.a: At dinner with Riya's parents last night.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling after the dinner?
qa.a: Harish felt confused and anxious, overthinking whether Riya's mother's mouth-only smile meant a dislike of Harish.

qa.q: What would you advise Harish to do?
qa.a: Treat the smiles as rough clues only, trust Riya's knowledge that her mother is shy, and simply ask Riya how her parents felt.

qa.q: How might Riya's mother have seen the evening?
qa.a: She may have been friendly but shy with a new person, smiling the way she smiles at everyone.

grounding: The email shows a young adult trying to read polite versus warm smiles and recognising the difference is only a rough clue.

passage:
Madhav, you asked what I learned working at the café near college. Okay, I'm Chetan, and mostly I learned about smiles.
First month, I thought I was an expert. Customers who smile with just their mouth, quick, then look at their phone: polite. Customers whose eyes crinkle, whose smile stays: genuinely happy. I even made a joke chart with my co-worker.
Then I got it wrong twice in one day. An old man who never smiled, just nodded, left me the kindest note on a napkin. And a woman who beamed at me, eyes and all, complained to the manager ten minutes later.
So now I think of it as a rough guess. Sometimes a real smile is tiny. Sometimes a polite one is really convincing.
These days, if I want to know if someone's happy with their coffee, I just ask. "Is it okay?" People usually tell you.

qa.q: What did the old man leave Chetan?
qa.a: The kindest note on a napkin.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling after getting it wrong twice in one day?
qa.a: Chetan felt humbled and a bit surprised, realising the smile chart was not reliable.

qa.q: What does Chetan do now to find out if customers are happy?
qa.a: Chetan treats smiles as a rough guess and simply asks, "Is it okay?"

qa.q: How might the old man have seen his own behaviour?
qa.a: The old man probably didn't smile much by nature but was genuinely pleased, which he showed through the note.

grounding: The spoken account shows a young adult learning that polite and genuine smiles are only rough clues, and asking directly instead.

passage: I share a college flat with Dilnaz and Ganga, so I was on the sofa when Dilnaz gave Ganga her birthday present: a watercolour of the pond in Ganga's village, which Dilnaz had worked on for two weeks. Ganga said, "Oh wow, thank you!" and smiled. It was a nice smile, but only her mouth moved, and it lasted about a second before she leaned the painting against the wall. Dilnaz's face flickered. Later, in the kitchen, Dilnaz whispered to me, "She hated it. Did you see? Mouth only." I honestly couldn't tell. Ganga is quiet about everything; she smiled the same way when she got her exam results. That night I saw Ganga sitting alone with the painting on her knees, touching the corner with the lotus, and her whole face was soft. I told Dilnaz. The next morning the painting was up on Ganga's wall, and Ganga said, "It's exactly the colour at dawn."

qa.q: How long had Dilnaz worked on the painting?
qa.a: Dilnaz had worked on it for two weeks.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she whispered 'She hated it'?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt hurt and anxious, reading the quick mouth-only smile as dislike; but that smile was only a rough clue, since Ganga smiles quietly about everything.

qa.q: What would be a wiser way for Dilnaz to read Ganga's reaction?
qa.a: Compare it with Ganga's usual quiet smile and simply ask, rather than judging from one brief expression.

qa.q: How did Ganga seem to feel about the painting later?
qa.a: Alone with it that night, Ganga looked soft and touched, then hung it up and said it was exactly the colour at dawn.

grounding: It shows a young adult reading a brief mouth-only smile as polite dislike when it was a quiet genuine one, so the cue works only as a rough clue.
